title: Spacewalkers Launch Final Phase of Multi-Year Space Station Power Upgrade【CBS News】
body:
Astronauts Shane Kimbrough and Megan McArthur stepped outside the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday, beginning the first of two meticulously planned spacewalks that will finish a multi‑year overhaul of the station’s aging power infrastructure. The pair installed the last set of roll‑out solar array blankets, known as iROSA, which will boost the station’s electrical output and extend the life of its solar‑power system well into the next decade.

The upgrade, now in its final phase, replaces the original 1998‑era solar panels with more efficient, modular arrays that can be added incrementally without shutting down the station’s power supply. Over the past three years, crews have performed a series of extravehicular activities (EVAs) to attach the new iROSA units to the truss structure, replace aging power converters, and re‑wire the station’s electrical grid. This latest EVA marks the completion of the hardware installation, after which ground controllers will run a series of tests to verify that the new panels are fully integrated and delivering the expected megawatts of power.

The significance of the iROSA upgrade extends beyond a simple boost in electricity. The ISS, now in its third decade of continuous human presence, relies on a delicate balance of power to support scientific experiments, life‑support systems, and the myriad of onboard computers that keep the habitat running. The original solar arrays, while groundbreaking at launch, have suffered gradual degradation from micrometeoroid impacts and prolonged exposure to the harsh space environment. By adding the newer, higher‑efficiency blankets—each capable of generating roughly 20 percent more power per unit area—the station can accommodate an expanding roster of experiments that demand higher energy loads, such as advanced materials research and Earth‑observation instruments.

The spacewalk itself lasted just over six hours, a testament to the crew’s training and the refined EVA procedures that NASA has honed since the early shuttle era. Kimbrough, a veteran of three previous spacewalks, and McArthur, who previously performed a spacewalk during the Crew‑2 mission, worked in tandem to unroll the thin, flexible solar fabric, secure it to the truss, and connect the power harnesses. Their successful deployment relied on a suite of robotic assistance from the station’s Canadarm2, which positioned the panels with millimetre precision, minimizing the physical strain on the astronauts and reducing the risk of contamination.

While the hardware is now in place, the final step will be a series of “power-up” tests conducted by mission control in Houston. Engineers will gradually shift the station’s power load from the legacy arrays to the new iROSA units, monitoring voltage stability, thermal performance, and the health of the newly installed power converters. If all parameters remain within design specifications, the ISS will achieve a net increase of roughly 2.5 megawatts of usable power—a margin that could prove crucial as the station prepares for upcoming commercial and research missions slated for the late 2020s.

Looking ahead, the successful completion of the iROSA upgrade underscores NASA’s broader strategy of extending the ISS’s operational lifespan while simultaneously paving the way for the next generation of orbital habitats. The added power capacity not only supports the current scientific agenda but also offers a buffer for future commercial modules, private‑sector experiments, and potentially even lunar‑orbiting platforms that may dock with the station. As the crew turns its focus to upcoming research campaigns, the refreshed power system will serve as a silent yet vital backbone, ensuring that humanity’s flagship laboratory in low Earth orbit remains a beacon of scientific discovery for years to come.
